name: heimdal
why: Alternative Kerberos 5 implementation; a real door into how authentication tickets actually work, though heavy to explore.

brief.what_it_is: Heimdal is a free implementation of Kerberos 5, the network authentication protocol that issues tickets so users and services can prove who they are. The README also lists ASN.1/DER and PKIX as areas it implements. The repository is C source built with GNU Autoconf and Automake. The brew formula installs a set of command-line tools, including kinit, klist, kdestroy, kadmin, kpasswd, ktutil, kgetcred, kswitch, hxtool, gsstool and krb5-config. The README does not describe what these tools take in or produce, and says only that man pages exist for most commands.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no stated motivation. It describes Heimdal as an implementation of ASN.1/DER, PKIX and Kerberos, and the GitHub topics add gssapi, krb5-kdc and pki-library.

brief.install_notes: Requirements from the wiki: a C compiler in loose ANSI C mode (gcc or clang), lex or flex, awk, yacc or bison, a socket library, Berkeley DB or a compatible replacement for building the server side, Perl with JSON.pm, and Python. Build with sh autogen.sh if from git, then ./configure, make and make install. Optional features include readline (falls back to editline), hesiod, IPv6 and OpenLDAP. The wiki also has a long cross-compilation section for NetBSD evbarm that uses a git URL at git://svn.h5l.org/heimdal.git. Nothing in the fetched pages mentions accounts, first-run setup or a Kerberos realm configuration step.
brief.standout: Heimdal is one of the two main free Kerberos 5 implementations, and this entry's point is that it is an alternative to MIT Kerberos. Its brew formula bundles many tools, including kf, otp and string2key, which the README does not explain. Pulling them apart is a way to see how tickets, keytabs and the credential cache fit together.
brief.status: unknown. The fetched pages show CI badges for Linux, macOS and Windows, about 31,212 commits, 371 stars and 204 forks. No release date or last-commit date appears in the text I fetched, so I cannot confirm recent activity.
brief.caveats: The README is thin and points to the wiki and project site for details. The fetched heimdal.software URL returned the same GitHub repository page rather than a separate project site. Server-side builds need Berkeley DB or an equivalent. Cross-compiling is involved and the wiki example is for NetBSD. The brew description calls it an alternative Kerberos 5 implementation, and the wiki's git URL may be out of date. The licence is in a LICENSE file that I did not open, so I cannot say which licence applies.

Bug reports and bugs are appreciated.

judge.reason: Kerberos tickets make authentication mechanics tangible, and Heimdal’s command-line tools offer a hands-on route into a foundational protocol most developers rarely inspect.

entry.title: Heimdal
entry.tldr: A free Kerberos 5 implementation whose bundled tools let you look at tickets, keytabs and credential caches, the machinery behind single sign-on.
entry.deeper_look:
Heimdal is an implementation of Kerberos 5, the network protocol in which a trusted server issues tickets so users and services can prove who they are without sending passwords around. The README describes it as an implementation of "ASN.1/DER, PKIX, and Kerberos", and the GitHub topics add gssapi, krb5-kdc and pki-library.

The brew formula installs a large set of command-line tools. The familiar ones are `kinit` (get a ticket), `klist` (list what you hold), `kdestroy`, `kpasswd`, `kadmin` and `ktutil`. Less obvious ones include `kgetcred`, `kswitch`, `hxtool`, `gsstool`, `string2key`, `otp` and `kf`. The README does not explain what these take in or produce, and says only that "There are man pages for most of the commands."

The README gives no stated motivation. What the brief does establish is that Heimdal is one of the two main free Kerberos 5 implementations, the alternative to MIT Kerberos. Reading its tools side by side is a way to see how tickets, keytabs and the credential cache fit together, which is a door into how authentication works on many corporate and university networks.
entry.install:
brew install heimdal
# Real use needs a Kerberos realm and a KDC to talk to. The brief found no first-run setup steps.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the options for requesting a ticket-granting ticket, the first step of Kerberos login.
Shows how to list the tickets in a credential cache.
Shows the build and link information the installed Kerberos library reports to programs.

entry.whats_unique: It is an independent second implementation of Kerberos 5, not MIT's, and it ships a wide set of small tools, including ones like `string2key` and `otp`, that expose individual pieces of the protocol.
entry.caveats: The README is thin and defers to a wiki, the brief could not confirm recent activity, and doing anything real requires a Kerberos realm and KDC to talk to.
